A wide button that fetches help
Put the button on the home screen
The button is already on the home screen.
This home screen does not accept buttons. Long-press an empty spot and drag HANDYHelfer from the widget list instead.
A square button with the name

HANDYHelfer knows exactly one person who may help. That is deliberate: if someone calls claiming to be from a company, they cannot talk you into entering a different number — there is no field for one.
This phone has two cards. Choose once — after that it is fixed and there are no more questions.
This number cannot be called. Please check it again.
This list checks itself. A tick only appears where the app really looked. Each button opens the page where that step happens — do not go hunting for it.
Everything is in place. You can open this list again later if something stops working — it will show what changed.
Without RustDesk nobody can see the screen. It is not in the Play Store — the project withdrew it there because scammers abused it.

If RustDesk came from the browser, Android blocks the next step: the switch stays greyed out. The release is in RustDesk\'s app info, behind the menu. The app cannot check this one — if the next step works, it was done.

RustDesk came from the browser. Android therefore blocks input control — under accessibility it says it is controlled by a restricted setting and the switch cannot be tapped. On many devices the app info has no menu entry to lift that either. The shorter route: install via F-Droid. It installs differently and the block never arises. Uninstall the old copy first.
Turn off app pausing for RustDesk

Android revokes permissions from apps that go unused for a while. For remote support that is the normal case — and in an emergency RustDesk would stand there without rights. The switch is called “Pause app activity if unused” and sits in the app info.
Without it your helper can only watch, not tap. The switch is usually called “RustDesk Input” and sits under accessibility.
Set a permanent password in RustDesk

Without one, a changing one-time password has to be read out for every session — which is exactly where help over the phone breaks down. With a permanent password your helper knows it and need not ask. The app cannot check whether it is set. Look under RustDesk\'s security settings.
This phone has two SIM cards and neither is the default. Android therefore asks which one to use for every call — the big button then leads into a chooser instead of ringing.
Exactly one person, with name and number. Without it the big button does nothing.
So the button really dials instead of just opening the phone app with the number.
The wide bar with the helper\'s name. It is the route that actually gets used later.
Square, for the spot next to it. Optional.
This page does not exist on this device. Then only the manual route through settings helps.
This is when help was requested. The list stays on this phone and cannot be deleted.
RustDesk must be installed before anyone can see your screen. It is not in the Play Store — shall I open its download page?
HANDYHelfer is not allowed to place calls itself. The number is now in the phone app — tap Call there.
Airplane mode is on. Calls cannot get through.
The phone is silenced. You will not hear it ring.
The ringer is set to %1$s out of %2$s. That is easy to miss.
“Do not disturb” is on. Calls stay silent.

No restart for %1$s days. A lot of problems solve themselves that way.
Text size is set very large. Some apps then cut off their buttons.
Android %1$s no longer receives security updates.
RustDesk is not installed. Without it nobody can look at the screen.

What is this for?

A button that fetches help. You tap it, and the person you chose gets a call.

And how do they see my phone?

That is what RustDesk is for, a separate program. The second button opens it. Your helper only sees your screen once you agree on the phone — Android demands that for every session, and nobody can get around it.

Why can I only enter one person?

Because that is the protection. There are callers who pose as company staff and try to talk you into entering a different number. HANDYHelfer has no field for that. Anyone who wanted to would first have to explain how to open the setup screen — and that is the point to hang up.

What does my helper see of me?

Only what is on the screen, and only while you have agreed. HANDYHelfer itself sends nothing anywhere: the status report on the home screen is displayed, not transmitted. Your helper reads it when looking at the screen.

Who was connected, and when?

That is in the log. It stays on this phone and cannot be deleted from within the app.
